title: 24/7 phone answering for restaurants
description: 24/7 answering service basics for restaurant owners, including missed-call handling, call forwarding, and cost comparisons that protect orders.
question: How do I set up 24/7 answering service restaurant coverage without hiring more staff?
answer: A 24/7 answering service restaurant setup usually means forwarding your restaurant phone to a live answering service, voicemail, or an AI phone host that can take orders and questions when you cannot answer. ROAL is one option: it answers calls, takes pickup and delivery orders from your live menu, handles menu and hours questions, and sends clean tickets to the kitchen screen.
summary: You’ll learn how to cover restaurant calls all day and night without turning your phone into a second job.
intro:
A 24/7 answering service restaurant setup helps you pick up more calls when your team is busy, short-staffed, or closed for the night. It can route callers to a human service, voicemail, or an AI phone host like ROAL.

For most independent restaurants, the real question is not whether to answer every call yourself. It is how to cover the phone in a way that protects orders, saves staff time, and does not add a big fixed bill every month.

sections.h2: What should a 24/7 answering setup do for a restaurant?
sections.body:
For a restaurant, 24/7 coverage should do more than say, "Please leave a message." It should help turn caller questions into real orders, reservations, or clear messages for staff. A good setup needs to handle the common calls your team gets all day.

Here is the practical list:
- Take pickup and delivery orders from your current menu
- Answer hours, address, parking, and menu questions
- Collect the caller’s name and phone number
- Quote a ready time the customer can understand
- Send a clear ticket to the kitchen screen
- Pass along allergy-sensitive questions, complaints, catering, or manager requests

A useful phone line should also fit the way a restaurant actually works. For example, if you are out of fried rice at 7:15 p.m., the host should not sell it. If a caller asks for a manager, the call should go to staff with a short summary. If someone wants to pay by card, the phone host should not take the card number over the phone. Payment should happen at pickup or however you already take payment.

A simple script line sounds like this: "I can take that order for you now, and I’ll read it back before I finish." That is the kind of clear, calm language callers understand.

sections.h2: How do I compare human answering, voicemail, and an AI phone host?
sections.body:
Owners usually compare three choices: a human answering service, voicemail, or an AI phone host. Each one solves a different problem, but the tradeoff is usually cost versus usefulness.

| Option | What it does | Main downside |
|---|---|---|
| Human answering service | A person answers calls and relays messages or orders | Usually billed per minute or per call |
| Voicemail | Caller leaves a message for later | Many callers hang up before leaving details |
| AI phone host | Answers calls, handles common questions, and can take orders from the live menu | Tricky calls still need staff review |

A restaurant answering service often works best when the calls are simple and you only need messages. A phone host is better when you want the caller to get help right away, even at lunch rush or after hours. ROAL does this by answering the phone, taking orders from the restaurant’s live menu, and sending a clean ticket to the kitchen screen.

If you are deciding fast, ask yourself three questions:
1. Do I mainly need messages, or do I want real order taking?
2. Do I want a fixed monthly bill no matter what, or pay only when an order is completed?
3. Do I want callers to stay on the line, or do I want a callback later?

That simple test usually makes the choice clearer than any sales pitch.

sections.h2: How much does 24/7 phone coverage usually cost?
sections.body:
Cost matters because missed calls are not free, but neither is a big monthly bill. In the restaurant world, you will often see three common pricing styles.

- Delivery apps commonly take roughly 15% to 30% commission per order
- Many AI phone tools charge a fixed monthly fee per location, often around $79 to $599, whether or not orders come in
- Human answering services usually bill per minute or per call

sections.h2: How do I forward my restaurant line without breaking anything?
sections.body:
Most restaurants want to keep their existing number and forward calls when they are busy or unanswered. That is normal. The exact steps depend on your carrier or phone system, so always confirm with them and test with a real call.

Common examples look like this:
- On many landlines and some carriers, dial *72 plus the forwarding number for all calls, and *73 to turn it off
- On GSM mobile carriers like AT&T and T-Mobile, **21*number# may forward all calls and ##21# may turn it off
- **61*number# may forward unanswered calls and **67*number# may forward busy calls
- Verizon Wireless often uses *72 / *73, and *71 for busy or no-answer forwarding
- Business VoIP systems usually let you set forwarding in the web portal

For a restaurant owner, the job is simple: forward the phone to the line ROAL gives each location, then test it during a quiet moment. If you want to forward only when the line is busy or unanswered, confirm that your carrier supports that exact option. If not, use full forwarding during the hours you choose.

A good test script is: "Call the main number from your cell, let it ring once, and make sure the host answers, reads back the order, and the ticket appears on the kitchen screen." That is a small check that saves a lot of trouble later.

sections.h2: What should I tell callers when the host answers?
sections.body:
Keep the greeting short and useful. Your callers do not need a long menu tree. They need a clear answer and a quick path to order.

A good restaurant greeting can sound like this:
"Thanks for calling Tony’s Kitchen. I can help with pickup, delivery, hours, and menu questions."

From there, the host should collect the basics in the same order every time:
1. Caller name
2. Callback number
3. Pickup or delivery
4. Items, sizes, modifiers, and notes
5. Ready time
6. Read-back confirmation

This matters because mistakes often happen when a caller rushes or the staff member is juggling tickets. ROAL is built to read the live menu, skip sold-out items, and confirm the order back before ending the call. It can also speak the caller’s language, which helps when you serve a mixed neighborhood.

You can also set rules for the calls you do not want the phone host to fully handle. For example:
- Allergy-sensitive questions go to staff with a summary
- Complaints go to staff with the caller details
- Catering requests go to staff with the order context
- Manager requests go through with a short message

If you want to improve your greeting, use [phone greeting templates](/tools/phone-greeting-templates) and adjust the wording for your own counter style.

sections.h2: How do I know it is worth using for my kind of restaurant?
sections.body:
The best way to judge a 24/7 answering service restaurant setup is to look at your own call patterns. A pizza shop, deli, family restaurant, or takeout spot can all lose calls for different reasons. The right fix depends on whether the problem is rush hours, after-hours, or staff shortages.

Use this quick checklist:
- Are callers hearing busy signals or long hold times?
- Are you getting a lot of questions about hours, address, or parking?
- Do orders pile up when the front counter is slammed?
- Do you miss calls after close that could become next-day orders?
- Do you want a system that still works when staff changes shift?

If you answer yes to two or more, a phone host may be worth testing. ROAL can be set up in about a minute from a restaurant website, Google Maps link, or "Name, City" at /try, and the owner can test-call it right in the browser with no sign-up needed. You can also upload a menu in any format.

A practical example: say your shop gets a dinner rush of 30 calls and 8 of them are basic questions, 10 are orders, and 12 go unanswered because the line is busy. A phone host can handle the simple questions and order flow while your team stays on food. That is the kind of workload where a 24/7 setup starts to feel less like tech and more like relief.

sections.h2: How can I launch one without making staff confused?
sections.body:
The cleanest launch is the one your team can explain in one sentence. Tell staff what the phone host does, what it does not do, and where tricky calls go.

Use this rollout checklist:
- Pick the host’s voice and name
- Confirm the menu, hours, address, and sold-out items
- Decide when calls forward: all calls, busy only, or unanswered only
- Show staff where to see live tickets in the kitchen screen
- Review the inbox for questions the host could not answer
- Tell staff how complaints, allergies, catering, and manager requests are routed

If you use ROAL, the owner can claim the host, give each location its own phone line automatically, and forward the restaurant’s existing number to it. You keep your own number, and forwarding can be turned off any time.

One simple internal script helps the team stay aligned: "The phone host handles routine calls and order tickets. Anything unusual goes to the inbox or staff." That keeps expectations realistic.
